newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada appeals ruling in missing stowaways case.
newsitem.headline: Canada appeals ruling in missing stowaways case.

text.p: A Canadian government prosecutor on Friday appealed a court ruling that upheld a decision which freed Taiwanese ship officers accused of killing three Romanian stowaways.

James Martin, a Canadian Crown prosecutor acting under direction from Canada's Justice department and on behalf of Romania, appeared in the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal on Friday to seek a reversal of a ruling made the day before by another appeals judge. Martin's appeal was delayed until March 20 because defence lawyers were not able to appear in court.

On Thursday Nova Scotia Supreme Court Judge Michael MacDonald freed six Taiwanese officers of the merchant ship Maersk Dubai who were accused of putting three Romanian stowaways overboard to meet their presumed deaths during two voyages in March and May 1996.
The officers were discharged from the court, but have been prevented from leaving Canada because police seized their passports as evidence last May.
Chin-Shiu Kuo, second mate on the Maersk Dubai, told Reuters on Friday he is afraid that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) has him under surveillance and may arrest him again.
"I don't feel safe. I don't feel free because they won't give me my travel documents," he said.
An RCMP spokesman told Reuters that police visited Kuo on Friday simply to notify him of Canada's appeal.

In his ruling, which came after a 41-day hearing, MacDonald said he did not have the jurisdiction to order the extradition of the accused officers to Romania to face murder charges. But MacDonald added that if he had such jurisdiction, he would have issued manslaughter and second-degree murder charges against the officers.
Shortly after MacDonald's decision, Canada lost its first bid before an appeals court judge to halt the officers' discharge.
In a statement issued through their lawyers, the Taiwanese officers called MacDonald's decison "bittersweet."

"It is a bittersweet victory. Sweet because the false accusations forcibly installed upon us were lifted and cleared at the end. It is bitter because ... we lost a year of our freedom," the officers said.

In what has become an international diplomatic tussle, Bucharest wants the officers extradited to Romania, while Taiwan says it has jurisdiction because the ship was operating in international waters under the Taiwanese flag.

Taiwanese officials said that if the men are allowed to leave Canada, they will face authorities in Taipei on the accusations. And China, which claims sovereignty over Taiwan, insists Beijing should decide the officers' fate.

The stowaway story broke last May when eight Filipino sailors fled the Maersk Dubai in this port city on Canada's Atlantic coast and accused the ship's officers of forcing the Romanians overboard. Acting on Romania's request, the RCMP stormed the ship and arrested the officers.
The bodies of the missing stowaways, Radu Danciu, 29, Petre Sangeorzan, 20, and Gheorghe Mihoc, 18, have not been found, and Romanian investigators said their families have not heard from them.
